short: Unofficial ceasefires broke out along the Western Front in the first winter of the war.
full:
On Christmas Eve 1914 German soldiers in parts of the Ypres salient set candles and small trees on their parapets and began singing carols. British troops opposite answered. Over the next two days unofficial truces spread along perhaps two-thirds of the British sector, and to French and Belgian stretches as well. Men climbed out of their trenches to bury the dead lying in no man's land, exchanged tobacco, buttons and rations, and in a few places kicked footballs about on the frozen ground.

The truces were local, unauthorised and short; in some sectors the shooting never stopped at all. Both high commands reacted with alarm, and orders issued before later Christmases threatened courts martial and scheduled bombardments to prevent a repeat. Nothing on the same scale happened again. The episode is remembered because it was so at odds with what followed: poison gas at Ypres four months later, and four more years of a war that killed some ten million soldiers.
